lessons.title: A first C++20 program
lessons.passage: Start here. No earlier C++ knowledge is required; the lessons introduce the source notation before asking you to change it. A program is a list of instructions for the computer. C++20 names the language version used in this course. The first example prints a greeting. You can run it in your browser without installing a compiler. Read the program from top to bottom. #include  asks the compiler to use the iostream header: a supplied file that makes text-output tools available. main names the starting group of instructions. int says this group reports a whole-number status when it finishes, and () means this example supplies no inputs to that group. The braces { and } enclose its instructions. A semicolon ; ends each instruction inside the braces. The prefix std:: identifies a name from the standard library, C++’s supplied collection of reusable tools. std::cout names the destination for normal text output. Think of << here as “send the text on the right to the output.” The double quotes mark literal text: characters to display rather than instructions to execute. Inside that text, \n means start a new line. It is two characters in the source spelling but requests one line break in the output. Run code first compiles the C++ source: it checks the language rules and translates the instructions into a runnable program. It then runs that program. A compiler diagnostic explains a problem in your source. If compilation fails, read the message beside Program output and correct the source before running again. The final instruction return 0; ends main and reports successful completion to the environment running the program.

lessons.title: Store numbers and calculate a result
lessons.passage: A variable gives a name to a stored value. In int apples = 20;, int is the type: it says this variable holds a whole number. apples is the name, and = 20 supplies its starting value. This starting step is called initialization. A later assignment can replace the stored value. The + operator adds two numbers. The program below stores two counts, adds them, and stores the answer as total. When std::cout receives a variable name without quotation marks, it prints that variable’s value. Quoted text such as "total=" is printed as text instead. Repeating << in one instruction sends successive pieces from left to right; the final quoted line-break sequence starts a new output line. A type has limits. int can store only a finite range of whole numbers; it is not an unlimited mathematical integer. These small counts are safely within that range. We will learn explicit limit checks later, after functions and decisions are familiar.

lessons.title: Give text a name
lessons.passage: A string is a value containing a sequence of characters, such as a person’s name. std::string is the standard-library type used here, made available by #include . A quoted literal is fixed text in the source; a string variable gives text a name so it can be read and changed while the program runs. We do not need to manage the storage for these ordinary variables. Several << operations in one output instruction send several pieces to the same destination, from left to right. In the last instruction below, one piece is quoted text, one is the current value of name, and the last is a line break.

lessons.title: Choose which instructions run
lessons.passage: A condition is a question whose answer is true or false. The comparison score >= 60 asks whether score is at least 60. The >= symbol includes equality. Use > for strictly greater than and == for equal to. bool is the C++ type for these two possible answers. An if statement runs its first group of instructions when the condition in parentheses is true. An else group runs when that condition is false. Braces keep the instructions for each choice together. Only one of these two groups runs on a single visit to this statement.

lessons.title: Repeat instructions with a while loop
lessons.passage: A loop repeats a group of instructions. A while loop checks its condition before every repetition, including the first. When the condition becomes false, execution continues after the loop’s closing brace. In this example count starts at 1. count <= 3 asks whether it is at most 3. The instruction count = count + 1 replaces it with the next whole number. This change eventually makes the condition false, giving the loop a way to stop. C++ also provides ++count as a shorter instruction for increasing count by one; either spelling performs this update when used as its own instruction.

lessons.title: Name a calculation with a function
lessons.passage: A function is a named group of instructions. A function call asks the computer to run those instructions. We have already used main as the program’s starting function; now we will write another function and call it from main. In int twice(int value), the first int says the function produces a whole-number result. twice is its name. The name value inside the parentheses is a parameter: a variable that receives the input for this call. return sends the calculated result back to the place that called the function. The expression twice(6) calls the function with 6 as its input. The function returns 12, which initializes answer. Multiplication uses * here. Describe a function’s contract in plain terms: this one accepts a small whole number and returns twice that number; very large inputs need range checks that this introductory version does not provide.

lessons.title: Keep several values in a vector
lessons.passage: A collection groups several values so a program can work with them together. std::vector is a standard-library type for a sequence of whole numbers. The  part says what kind of element each position contains. #include  makes this type available. The braces in std::vector scores{70, 80, 90}; give the starting elements. scores.push_back(100) calls an operation on that vector to append one element. The dot connects the variable to an operation it provides. scores.size() asks how many elements are currently present. A range-based for loop visits each element. In for (int score : scores), score receives the next element’s value each time through the loop. This differs from the earlier while loop: the vector determines which values to visit, so we do not maintain a counter ourselves.

lessons.title: A value parameter gives independent state

lessons.title: References borrow; const restricts access
lessons.passage: Ownership means responsibility for keeping a resource available and releasing it when finished. A resource can be memory or an open file. Borrowing means using something without taking that cleanup responsibility; the owner must keep it alive while it is used. A reference is an alias for an existing object. It does not own that object and does not extend the lifetime of an arbitrary referred-to value. A reference parameter is useful when a function needs to update a caller-owned value. Make mutation explicit in the interface. A const reference provides read-only access through that reference, while returning a value gives the caller an independent result. Prefer those independent values when borrowing would make lifetimes difficult to reason about.

lessons.title: RAII ties cleanup to scope
lessons.passage: RAII means acquiring a resource as part of an object’s initialization and releasing it in its destructor. The resource might be memory, a file, or a lock.
